source.title: GENERator: A Long-Context Generative Genomic Foundation Model
source.authors: Wei Wu; Qiu-Yi Li; Yuan-Yuan Zhang; Zhi-Hao Zhan; Ruipu Chen; Mingyang Li; Kun Fu; Jun-Yan Qi; Yongzhou Bao; Chao Wang; Yiheng Zhu; Zhiyun Zhang; Jian Tang; Fu-Li Feng; Jie-Ping Ye; Yuwen Liu; Hui Xiong; Zheng Wang

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including supplementary figures and tables.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports that pre-training losses vary with corpus and tokenizer and argues that biological sequence models may not follow natural-language scaling trends. It does not fit power laws or test compute-optimal allocations.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure held-out cross-entropy scaling laws or compute-optimal parameter/token splits. Its pre-training-loss comparisons bear on setup sensitivity (V7), while its parameter-scale sequence-recovery comparison is a performance result, not a test of a power law. The discussion's broader scaling claim cites other work; cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is a genomic model paper with no scaling sweep, no power-law fit, no extrapolation test and no compute-optimal allocation. Its loss comparisons change the training corpus (functional vs all-sequence) or the tokenizer (vocabulary size). Neither bears on fitted exponents or the compute-optimal split that V7 names. The paper itself says tokenizer losses are inherently incomparable. The 1B vs 3B comparison has only two sizes and uses downstream metrics. The only general scaling claim is in the Discussion, and it rests on cited work (ProteinGym, a blog post, Kaplan et al.). So the paper discusses scaling but does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that data curation, tokenization and architecture, rather than scale alone, drive genomic model quality. In the Discussion they assert, citing ProteinGym, a blog post and Kaplan et al., that biological sequence models do not show consistent scaling trends and saturate near 10B parameters. That claim is cited, not tested here.
record.recipe_differences: This is a genomic-model study with pre-training-loss comparisons and sequence-recovery evaluations, not a reproduction of the original language-model scaling-law experiments or compute-optimal allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported pre-training loss varies with training-corpus composition and tokenizer; the authors also note that tokenizer differences make raw losses incomparable.

fits_no_version.finding: GENERator-All, trained on about 2T nucleotides of all-sequence data, reaches lower pre-training loss than functional-sequence GENERator-1B. Yet it does worse on downstream tasks, e.g. revised NT tasks and Gener tasks (Tables S3–S6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In genomic LMs, lower pre-training loss obtained by changing corpus composition need not mean better downstream performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Pre-training loss across k-mer/BPE tokenizers ranges from about 1 (1-mer) to much higher (8-mer). The authors call these losses incomparable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Raw pre-training loss is not comparable across tokenizers with different vocabulary sizes in DNA LMs.

fits_no_version.finding: GENERator-3B beats 1B on sequence recovery (0.561 vs 0.515) and on ClinVar AUROC (0.921 vs 0.910). Embedding clustering also improves qualitatively with size and context length.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within the GENERator family, the larger model performs better on zero-shot genomic tasks; two sizes only.

record.problems: No held-out loss scaling sweep, power-law fit, extrapolation test, or compute-optimal allocation experiment. Loss comparisons vary corpus or tokenizer, and the paper states that tokenizer losses are not comparable. The discussion's general claim about biological scaling trends cites external work rather than testing it here.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows bearing on the claim were identified. The paper's embedding-clustering scale observations and cited external scaling results are not measures of the claim versions.

untested.parts: No loss sweep over parameters, tokens or compute; no power-law fit.
No small-run fit or extrapolation to larger runs.
No fixed-parameter depth/width comparison. The Mamba vs transformer comparison uses a downstream metric and compares architecture families, not shape.
Genomic models are trained, but no loss-vs-scale power-law form is examined.
Only two model sizes (1B, 3B) on downstream tasks; no predictability fit against scale or loss.
No exponents or compute-optimal splits are fitted, so their dependence on data, tokenizer or fitting method is not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T5/'tests' and the V7 'supports' label are dropped. Corpus- and tokenizer-driven loss differences are not evidence about how fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits depend on setup. The Kaplan citation appears only in the Discussion's cited claim about biological models.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pre-training loss sweep across parameters, tokens, or compute; no power-law fits.
No small-run fits or tests of predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or fitted parameter/token scaling with compute.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The paper studies genomic models but does not test whether their losses follow a power law; it does not test other modalities or repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling laws.
No study of downstream-task performance as a predictable function of scale or pre-training loss.

The study compares loss under different training-data and tokenizer setups, but does not fit exponents, test fitting-method sensitivity, examine curve bending with scale, or measure compute-optimal allocations.

rows.subject: GENERator-All
rows.size_stated: 1.2B (Table S15; Figure S6 names the comparator GENERator-1B)
rows.operation_detail: Pre-trained with all available eukaryotic RefSeq sequence rather than the functional-sequence corpus.
rows.baseline: GENERator-1B trained on functional sequences; exact loss not stated
rows.value: Lower pre-training loss; exact value not stated
rows.note: The authors say the lower loss reflects data composition, including easy-to-predict repetitive and ambiguous sequence, and does not indicate better downstream performance. Figure S6 plots the curves but exact values are not reported.
rows.check: Training-loss curves on two different corpora (functional vs all-sequence) are not held-out loss on a common set. Corpus composition is not a parameter, token or compute axis, and no exponent is fitted. This does not measure V7's fit-dependence. It is better treated as a fits_no_version finding.

rows.subject: Tokenizer comparison models (k-mer k=1–8, BPE vocabularies 512–8192, and Mamba+1mer)
rows.operation_detail: Compared pre-training loss trajectories across tokenizer configurations and Mamba+1mer.

conditions.value: k-mer k=1–8, BPE vocabularies 512–8192, and Mamba+1mer

rows.value: Loss ranges from roughly 1 for 1-mer to significantly higher for 8-mer; exact values not stated
rows.note: The authors state that different prediction-vocabulary sizes make these loss values inherently incomparable, motivating sequence recovery as their cross-tokenizer metric. The reported range is an aggregate description, not separate values for each tokenizer.
rows.check: Loss differences across tokenizers come from prediction-space size (4-way to 65536-way), as the authors say. The study uses this only to justify its sequence-recovery metric, not as a scaling-law fit result. There are no per-tokenizer values and no exponents, so it does not bear on V7.

rows.subject: GENERator-3B
rows.operation_detail: Compared sequence-recovery accuracy for GENERator-3B with GENERator-1B.

conditions.value: overall average across six taxonomic groups

rows.note: A two-size performance comparison; it does not measure held-out loss or establish a power-law relationship.
rows.check: A two-point size comparison (0.515 vs 0.561 overall sequence recovery) on a downstream metric. It cannot show predictable scaling (V6) or a power law. Correctly unlinked.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Pre-training loss comparisons across the tested corpus and tokenizer setups
reader_labels.reason: The reported loss changes with corpus choice and tokenizer, and the authors caution that tokenization-based loss values are not directly comparable (r1, r2); exponents and compute-optimal splits were not tested.
